plain_english: If someone handed your body over to a random stranger, you'd be furious. So why aren't you ashamed when you hand your mind over to any critic who comes along, letting them mess with your head and confuse you?
original_excerpt:
If a person had delivered up your body to some passer-by, you would certainly be angry. And do you feel no shame in delivering up your own mind to any reviler, to be disconcerted and confounded?

XXIX[2]

plain_english: Before you start anything, think about what it will take and what could go wrong. Then decide if you want to do it. Otherwise you'll start with excitement but quit when things get hard. "I want to win at the Olympics." Fine. But think about what that means first. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll have to stick to a special diet and give up treats. You'll have to train your body at set times, whether you feel like it or not, in hot weather and cold. You can't drink cold water or sometimes any wine at all. You have to do whatever your trainer says, like he's your doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in the dirt, hurt your arm, twist your ankle, eat dust, get beaten up, and still lose. If you think through all of this and still want to do it, go ahead. Otherwise, notice that you're acting like kids who play wrestler one day, gladiator the next, then pretend to blow trumpets or act in plays after they see a show. That's what you'll be like — wrestler one day, gladiator the next, philosopher today, public speaker tomorrow. But you won't be serious about any of it. Like a monkey, you'll copy whatever you see. You'll get excited about one thing after another, but lose interest as soon as the novelty wears off.
original_excerpt: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. “I would conquer at the Olympic Games.” But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat. Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar.

plain_english: You never think anything through carefully. You don't survey the whole situation and test it first. Instead, you jump in carelessly with half-hearted effort. Some people hear a philosopher speak—someone like Euphrates (though who could speak like him?)—and suddenly decide they want to be philosophers too. Think first, man. What does this actually involve? What can your nature handle? If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd check your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living like you do now and be a philosopher? Keep eating, drinking, getting angry, and complaining like before? You'll have to stay alert. You'll have to work hard. You'll have to control certain desires. You'll have to leave your friends behind. Your servant will look down on you. People will laugh at you. You'll lose out on everything—jobs, honors, court cases. Think through all of this completely. Then approach philosophy if you want—if you're willing to give up these things to buy peace, freedom, and calm. If not, don't bother. Don't be like children who play philosopher one day, tax collector the next, then speaker, then government official. These roles don't mix. You must be one person, either good or bad. Either develop your own reasoning or chase external things. Focus either on what's inside you or what's outside you. Be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.
original_excerpt: For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal. Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates[3]—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals. When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar’s officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
